oe.title: pH of water at different temperatures (pH meter faulty or not?)
points: Water self-ionises: the equilibrium lies far to the left, and K_w = [H_3O^+][OH^−] = 1.0 × 10^−14 at 25 °C only.
The ionisation of water is endothermic (bonds broken), so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium right and K_w increases.
[H_3O^+] increases with temperature, so pH falls below 7 at higher temperature. That fits the trend 7.08 → 6.92 → 6.63, so the meter may be fine.
The water is still neutral, because [H_3O^+] = [OH^−] at every temperature: neutral pH is only 7.00 at 25 °C.
7.08 at 20 °C (slightly above 7) is consistent with K_w being smaller below 25 °C.
Possible meter/experimental faults: not calibrated with buffer solutions (pH 4/7/10), no temperature compensation, dissolved CO_2 lowering pH, impure/non-deionised water, electrode not rinsed.
A check: recalibrate with standard buffers at each temperature and repeat with freshly boiled (CO_2-free) deionised water.
equations: K_w = [H_3O^+][OH^−]; for pure water [H_3O^+] = √K_w and pH = −log[H_3O^+]
diagrams: Sketch graph of K_w (or pH of pure water) against temperature: K_w rising, pH falling.

oe.title: "Chemistry is all about electrons" — comment
points: Electronic structure (aufbau, Hund, Pauli; s, p, d, f orbitals) explains the shape of the periodic table and periodic trends (ionisation energy, electronegativity).
Bonding is the sharing (covalent, σ/π, hybrid orbitals, dative) or transfer (ionic) of electrons. VSEPR uses electron pairs to predict shapes.

Redox reactions are electron transfer. Oxidation states and electrochemistry describe where the electrons go.
Organic mechanisms are drawn with curly arrows showing electron-pair movement (nucleophiles donate, electrophiles accept; homolytic vs heterolytic fission).
Acids/bases: the Lewis definition is electron-pair donation/acceptance; ligands donate lone pairs to metal ions.
Counterpoint: chemistry also involves the nucleus (isotopes in mass spectrometry, ^1H spin in NMR), energetics/entropy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS) and kinetics, so 'all' is an overstatement.

oe.title: How cimetidine, ranitidine and burimamide counteract histamine
points: Histamine acts as an agonist: it binds to (H_2) receptors on stomach cells, triggering acid secretion.
The three drugs are antagonists: they bind to the same receptor but produce no response, blocking histamine from binding.
They share structural features with histamine (pharmacophore): an imidazole ring (or similar heterocycle) and a nitrogen-containing chain of similar length and shape, so they fit the binding site.

Binding is by intermolecular forces/interactions: hydrogen bonds (N–H, C=N, NO_2, S groups), ionic interactions and London dispersion forces between drug functional groups and the receptor's amino-acid side chains.
Differences from histamine (e.g. a non-basic thiourea/guanidine-type group instead of –NH_2, a longer chain) mean they bind more strongly or for longer but don't activate the receptor.
Comparing structures identifies the common fragment responsible for binding (structure–activity relationship).

oe.title: Why these animals have different coloured blood
points: The colour comes from transition metal complexes: Fe^2+ in haemoglobin and chlorocruorin, Cu in haemocyanin.
In a complex the ligands split the five degenerate d orbitals into two energy levels; the gap Δ depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands (spectrochemical series).
A d–d transition absorbs a photon whose energy equals Δ (from the visible region). The colour seen is the complementary colour of the light absorbed.
Haemoglobin vs chlorocruorin: same metal ion (Fe^2+) but different porphyrin side groups (–CHO vs –CH=CH_2), changing Δ, so red vs green.
Haemocyanin uses a different metal (Cu, d^9) and histidine (imidazole N) ligands, so it has a different Δ and is blue when oxygenated.
The conjugated porphyrin ring also absorbs visible light (HOMO→LUMO / charge transfer), contributing to the colour.
Binding O_2 as a ligand changes the complex and so changes the colour (e.g. oxygenated vs deoxygenated blood).
equations: ΔE = hc/λ (per photon) or E = Lhc/λ (per mole)
Example: absorbing 530 nm (green) light: E = 6.02 × 10^23 × 6.63 × 10^−34 × 3.00 × 10^8/530 × 10^−9 = 226 kJ mol^−1, so red is seen
diagrams: d-orbital splitting diagram for an octahedral complex showing Δ and an electron being promoted.

oe.title: Strengths and weaknesses of the simple (Bohr-type) atom model
points: Strengths: shows a small dense nucleus of protons + neutrons, with electrons outside. It explains atomic number, isotopes, mass number and charge.
Electron shells (energy levels) explain quantised energy and line spectra (transitions between levels), and group/period trends and simple ionic/covalent bonding (dot-and-cross).
Weaknesses: electrons are not in fixed circular orbits. Quantum theory describes orbitals as regions of high probability, with wave behaviour.
Shells are split into subshells (s, p, d, f) with different shapes and energies; four quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s) describe each electron; aufbau, Hund's rule and Pauli exclusion apply.
The model can't explain shapes (VSEPR uses electron pairs), hybridisation (sp, sp^2, sp^3), σ and π bonds from orbital overlap, or molecular orbitals (bonding/antibonding, HOMO/LUMO).
It can't explain 4s filling before 3d, the extra stability of half-full/full subshells (Cr, Cu), or d-orbital splitting and colour in complexes.
It shows nothing of electron spin or the multiple lines (fine structure) in spectra.
equations: E = hf — quantised transitions give discrete lines
diagrams: Shapes of s and p (and d) orbitals.
Orbital box diagram showing Hund's rule.
Sigma vs pi bond orbital overlap sketch; energy level diagram showing subshells.

oe.title: How a stain remover (H_2O_2) works on coloured stains
points: The stain molecules are coloured because they contain conjugated systems (alternating single/double bonds, aromatic rings, C=O): chromophores.
Delocalised electrons mean a small HOMO–LUMO gap; absorbing visible light promotes electrons HOMO→LUMO and the complementary colour is seen (e.g. lycopene red).
Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising agent: it attacks C=C double bonds and phenolic –OH groups, breaking the conjugated system.
With shorter conjugation the HOMO–LUMO gap gets larger, so absorption moves into the UV and the product is colourless.
Products can be smaller, more polar molecules (e.g. containing –OH or C=O) that are more water-soluble and wash out.

Other components: surfactants/detergents (polar head and non-polar tail) lift non-polar stains like lycopene, and enzymes break down biological stains. Alkaline conditions deprotonate phenols (anthocyanins change colour/solubility).
equations: H_2O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^− → 2H_2O (H_2O_2 is reduced; the stain is oxidised)
ΔE = hc/λ: larger ΔE → shorter λ absorbed (UV) → colourless

oe.title: Factors when selecting chemicals for a titration
points: Primary standard: high purity, stable (doesn't absorb water/CO_2 from air or decompose), soluble, accurately known formula, reasonably high GFM (reduces weighing uncertainty). E.g. anhydrous Na_2CO_3, potassium hydrogen phthalate, K_2Cr_2O_7, oxalic acid. NaOH is not suitable.
Solutions that aren't primary standards (NaOH, KMnO_4, EDTA) must be standardised against a primary standard.
The reaction must be fast, go to completion, and have known stoichiometry (balanced equation).

There must be a clear end point: choose an indicator whose pH range lies in the vertical part of the titration curve (strong acid/strong base: most indicators; weak acid/strong base: phenolphthalein; strong acid/weak base: methyl orange). Some reactions are self-indicating (KMnO_4).
Indicator choice: pK_In should be close to the end-point pH (colour change roughly pK_In ± 1).

Suitable concentrations give a titre of a sensible size (~20–25 cm^3). Back titration if the analyte is insoluble or reacts slowly; complexometric (EDTA) titration for metal ions; redox titration for oxidising/reducing agents.
Safety and cost: choose less toxic/corrosive chemicals where possible.
equations: n = c × V; e.g. Na_2CO_3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H_2O + CO_2
Indicator: HIn ⇌ H^+ + In^−, K_In = [H^+][In^−]/[HIn]; colour changes when pH ≈ pK_In ± 1

oe.title: Isomerism in chemical synthesis and drug action
points: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements, so different functional groups and properties. A synthesis must give the correct one (e.g. Markovnikov's rule decides major/minor products).
Geometric (cis/trans) isomers arise from restricted rotation about C=C (or in rings) with two different groups on each carbon; they have different physical/chemical properties and shapes.

Optical isomers (enantiomers) arise from a chiral centre (4 different groups): non-superimposable mirror images. They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions; otherwise identical properties in non-chiral environments.
SN1 at a chiral centre gives a racemic mixture (planar carbocation attacked from either side). SN2 gives inversion, so the mechanism controls the stereochemistry of the product.
Receptors and enzyme active sites are chiral, so drug action depends on 3D shape: one enantiomer may be active and the other inactive or harmful (e.g. thalidomide).
So syntheses aim for a single enantiomer (stereoselective routes or separation). Polarimetry checks optical purity.

oe.title: Mixtures from addition reactions and how to isolate the products
points: Unsymmetrical alkenes + HX/H_2O give two structural isomers. Markovnikov: the major product comes via the more stable (more substituted) carbocation, e.g. propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (major) + 1-bromopropane (minor).
Addition at a C=C can create a chiral centre. The planar carbocation is attacked from either side, giving a racemic mixture (no net optical rotation).
Adding to dienes/alkynes: partial addition to an alkyne gives an alkene, which can be cis or trans (geometric isomers); further addition gives saturated products.
Halogen addition via a cyclic halonium ion gives anti addition (e.g. trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane).

Isolation: fractional distillation (structural isomers have different b.p. due to different intermolecular forces), chromatography (TLC/column/GC, different R_f), recrystallisation for solids, solvent extraction (separating funnel).
Enantiomers have identical physical properties, so they can't be separated by distillation; they need a chiral method (e.g. reacting with a single enantiomer or chiral chromatography).
Identify/confirm with IR, ^1H NMR, mass spectrometry, melting point and polarimetry.
diagrams: Curly-arrow mechanism showing primary vs secondary carbocations.
Enantiomers of butan-2-ol (wedge/dash mirror images).
Fractional distillation apparatus or a TLC plate showing separated products.

oe.title: Ways of representing electrons to explain concepts and reactions
points: Orbital box notation shows spin and Hund's rule/Pauli principle (half-filled stability in Cr/Cu, unpaired electrons → paramagnetism, d-electron counts in complexes).
Spectroscopic notation (1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 …) is compact for writing configurations and predicting blocks/ions (e.g. 4s lost before 3d).
Four quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s) uniquely describe each electron (Pauli exclusion).
Dot-and-cross and Lewis structures count bonding and lone pairs, which feed into VSEPR shapes and dative bonds (ligands).
Curly arrows show movement of electron pairs in mechanisms (nucleophilic substitution, electrophilic addition); fish-hook (half) arrows show homolytic fission and free radicals.

Energy level diagrams explain emission/absorption spectra (E = hf); d-orbital splitting diagrams explain colour of complexes; MO/HOMO–LUMO diagrams explain bonding/antibonding orbitals, bond order and colour of conjugated molecules.
Each representation has limits: no single one is 'most useful'. The best choice depends on the concept being explained.
equations: Bond order = ½(bonding e^− − antibonding e^−)
diagrams: Orbital box diagram, e.g. Fe^3+ [Ar] 3d^5.
Curly-arrow SN2 mechanism and fish-hook homolytic fission.
Octahedral d-orbital splitting diagram; HOMO–LUMO diagram.

oe.title: Confirming that blue crystals are CuSO_4.5H_2O
points: Water of crystallisation: heat a weighed sample to constant mass (cool in a desiccator). Blue → white anhydrous CuSO_4; the mass loss should match 5H_2O (36.0% water). Adding water back turns it blue again.
Copper: AAS, or colorimetry. Add excess NH_3 to give deep blue [Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^2+ and read from a calibration graph. A flame test gives blue-green.
Sulfate: add BaCl_2(aq) to get a white BaSO_4 precipitate; weigh it (gravimetric) to find % sulfate.
Copper by redox titration: Cu^2+ + excess KI → I_2, titrate with standard thiosulfate (starch indicator). Or complexometric EDTA titration.
Compare % composition with theoretical values (GFM 249.7 g: Cu 25.4%, SO_4 38.5%, H_2O 36.0%).
The colour comes from d–d transitions of Cu^2+ (d^9) in [Cu(H_2O)_6]^2+: it absorbs orange/red light, so it looks blue.
equations: Example: 2.50 g → 1.60 g after heating: water = 0.90 g (0.050 mol), CuSO_4 = 0.0100 mol → ratio 1:5

oe.title: Equilibria in acid–base indicators and buffers
points: Indicator: weak acid HIn ⇌ H_3O^+ + In^− with different colours (bromothymol blue: HIn yellow, In^− blue). Adding acid shifts it left (yellow); adding alkali removes H_3O^+ and shifts it right (blue) — Le Chatelier.
The colour change happens when [HIn] = [In^−], i.e. pH = pK_In, over about pK_In ± 1. Choose an indicator whose range falls in the steep part of the titration curve.
Acidic buffer: weak acid + its salt. The weak acid is only partially dissociated, and the salt supplies a large reservoir of conjugate base.

Added H_3O^+ combines with CH_3COO^− (equilibrium shifts left). Added OH^− reacts with H_3O^+, and more CH_3COOH dissociates to replace it (shifts right). The [acid]/[salt] ratio barely changes, so pH stays nearly constant.
Buffers are used to calibrate pH meters and to control pH in biological/industrial reactions. Basic buffers use a weak base + its salt (NH_3/NH_4Cl).
equations: Example: equal concentrations of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate → pH = pK_a = 4.76
diagrams: Titration curve with indicator range shaded.
Equilibrium diagrams with arrows showing the shift on adding H_3O^+ or OH^−.

oe.title: Oxidation state and colour in manganese species
points: Colour in transition metal compounds usually comes from d–d transitions: ligands split the d orbitals, an electron absorbs visible light to jump to a higher d orbital, and we see the complementary colour.

Mn^2+ (+2) is 3d^5 high spin: every d orbital already holds one electron with parallel spin, so any d–d transition would need a spin flip. These transitions are 'forbidden', absorption is extremely weak, and the ion looks (almost) colourless.
MnO_2 (+4) is 3d^3: d–d transitions are allowed. As a solid it absorbs strongly right across the visible spectrum, so it looks black.

MnO_4^− (+7) is 3d^0: there are no d electrons, so the colour cannot come from d–d transitions. It comes from charge transfer: electrons move from O ligand orbitals to empty Mn d orbitals, absorbing yellow-green light (about 525–550 nm), so it looks purple.
So there is no simple link between oxidation state and colour: what matters is the d-electron configuration and the type of electronic transition possible.
Higher oxidation states make Mn more electron-attracting (oxidising), which makes ligand-to-metal charge transfer easier. That is why the highest oxidation state shows the most intense colour.
equations: E = hc/λ links the absorbed wavelength to the energy gap ΔE
Example: MnO_4^− absorbs about 530 nm (green), so the transmitted colour is purple (complementary)
diagrams: Orbital box diagrams for Mn^2+, Mn^4+ and Mn(VII).
Octahedral d-orbital splitting diagram showing a d–d transition, and why high-spin d^5 needs a spin flip.

oe.title: Why theobromine and caffeine have a similar 'feel-good' effect
points: Drugs work by binding to receptors (or enzymes) in the body. A drug's effect depends on its shape and on the functional groups that interact with the binding site: the pharmacophore.

Theobromine and caffeine share the same fused-ring (xanthine/purine) skeleton, with the same C=O groups, ring N atoms and N-methyl groups in matching positions. They differ only by one CH_3 (caffeine) in place of an N–H (theobromine).

So both molecules have almost the same shape and size and fit the same receptor binding site. Both act on adenosine receptors; they are antagonists, blocking adenosine, which normally causes drowsiness.
Binding interactions: hydrogen bonds from C=O groups and N atoms (and N–H in theobromine) to the receptor, plus London dispersion forces from the flat ring system and the methyl groups.

The small difference (an N–H that can donate a hydrogen bond, versus N–CH_3) slightly changes binding strength and solubility. That explains why the strength of the effect differs while the type of effect is similar.
equations: Agonist: binds and triggers a response; antagonist: binds and blocks the natural molecule
diagrams: Both structures side by side with the common pharmacophore circled.
Sketch of the molecule in a receptor site with hydrogen bonds shown as dashed lines.
Lock-and-key style diagram of a drug blocking a receptor.
